content:
I discovered a feature in the System Settings app today that's been hiding in plain sight: you can set a different default language for each individual Mac app. If you already knew this, there's nothing to see here, please move on. But if you didn't, read on to find out how it works (and what doesn't)...

In reality, there are many bilingual people who have to switch between different languages throughout the day depending on who they're talking to or what they're doing. I don't have that problem, but I do often need to switch between British English (i.e., English...) and American English.

(Just to be clear, this is meant as a friendly joke! British English does differ from American English in some ways—for example, words ending in -ize in American English become -ise in British English. And, as James Nicoll put it: 'The problem with defending the purity of the English language is that English is about as pure as a cribbage whore. We don't just borrow words; on occasion, English has pursued other languages down alleyways to beat them unconscious and rifle their pockets for new vocabulary.')"

Switching between the two means I can't rely on spell check to catch cases where I've used the right word but the wrong language variant. I always assumed this was something I'd have to handle manually, but today I discovered there's at least a partial solution.

Hidden at the bottom of System Settings > General > Language & Region is an "Applications" section. You can add apps here and select a language. Apple's US-centric bias is on full display here: British English appears as "English (UK)" and American English as "English — English".

In my own case, since most of my writing happens in a browser, I use two different browsers depending on the target language. I have British English set as the system language, so Safari uses British English, while Chrome (which appears alphabetically in the list as Google Chrome) is set to American English.

However, as far as I can tell, there's an important caveat: you can only do this for apps that support macOS's localization/language APIs, so not every app will appear in the list.

If I'm the last person on Earth to discover this, feel free to laugh at me in the comments in whatever languages your multilingual eyes can manage.
